market_context: United States/international; refrigerated cold-smoked and hot-smoked salmon products.
title: Smoked Salmon: Is It Raw or Cooked, and How Is It Made?

seo.title: Smoked Salmon: Is It Raw or Cooked? Cold vs. Hot Smoked
seo.meta_description: Cold-smoked salmon is salted or cured and smoked at low temperatures that do not provide a full cooking kill step, so it retains a silky cured texture. Hot-smoked salmon is heated enough to cook the fish. Both are ready-to-eat, but refrigerated cold-smoked salmon requires special Listeria awareness.
seo.search_intent: Understand whether smoked salmon is raw or cooked, how cold and hot smoking differ, how the products are made, and which food-safety risks matter.

excerpt: “Smoked salmon” can describe two very different processes. Cold-smoked salmon is cured with salt and exposed to smoke at low temperature without a full cooking treatment, leaving a silky texture similar to cured raw fish. Hot-smoked salmon receives enough heat to cook and coagulate the fish proteins, producing a firm, flaky texture. Refrigerated cold-smoked salmon is ready-to-eat but deserves particular attention because of Listeria risk.
content_html:
It depends on the process: cold-smoked salmon is not cooked like a baked fillet, while hot-smoked salmon receives enough heat to cook the fish. Both use salt and smoke, but their temperature profiles and final textures are very different.

Labels may use terms such as cold-smoked, Nova-style, lox, hot-smoked, or kippered depending on the product and market.

Cold smoking uses relatively low temperatures

Salmon is typically dry-cured or brined first. Salt lowers water activity, seasons the fish, and changes texture.

The fish is then exposed to smoke in a relatively cool chamber. FDA describes cold-smoking conditions that do not provide a heat treatment sufficient to reliably inactivate vegetative pathogens.

The result remains soft, translucent, and silky rather than flaky.

Hot smoking actually cooks the fish

Hot smoking uses a warmer chamber and brings the center of the fish to a validated time-temperature combination that coagulates proteins and reduces vegetative pathogens.

FDA cites processes reaching approximately 145 °F (62.8 °C) for a sustained period as an example.

The finished salmon flakes apart much like conventionally cooked fish.

Curing and smoking are not the same process

Traditional lox refers to salt-cured salmon and historically does not require smoke. Nova-style salmon usually combines curing with cold smoking.

Modern labels are not always used consistently, so process wording is more useful than relying on the product name alone.

Gravlax is another example: it is cured with salt, sugar, and herbs but is not necessarily smoked.

Smoke adds flavor and some preservative effects

Smoke contains phenolic and carbonyl compounds that contribute aroma, surface color, and some antimicrobial and antioxidant activity.

Salt, partial drying, vacuum packaging, and refrigeration work together as preservation hurdles.

These hurdles do not make refrigerated cold-smoked salmon sterile.

Listeria is the key concern in refrigerated smoked seafood

Listeria monocytogenes can grow slowly at refrigerator temperatures. Because cold-smoked salmon lacks a final lethal cooking step, contamination can survive.

FDA treats refrigerated smoked seafood as a higher-concern ready-to-eat food for pregnant people, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems.

U.S. guidance for these groups recommends avoiding refrigerated smoked seafood unless it is used in a cooked dish.

Hot-smoked salmon still needs refrigeration

A validated heating step reduces pathogens present during smoking, but contamination can occur later during slicing, handling, or packaging.

Hot-smoked salmon is therefore still a perishable ready-to-eat food with a limited refrigerated shelf life.

Package swelling, abnormal odor, or poor temperature history are reasons to discard it.

Nutritionally it remains salmon, with more sodium

Smoked salmon retains protein and much of salmon's omega-3 fat, while curing usually raises sodium substantially.

Moisture loss can also concentrate nutrients per 100 grams.

Products vary based on brine strength, sugar, fish fat content, and drying.

How to identify what you are buying

Cold-smoked salmon is usually sold as thin silky slices. Hot-smoked salmon is more often a thicker, firm piece that flakes when pressed.

The practical rule: cold smoking cures and smokes salmon without a complete cooking kill step; hot smoking cooks it. Both can be ready-to-eat, but refrigerated cold-smoked salmon requires particular Listeria awareness.

faq.question: Is cold-smoked salmon raw?
faq.answer: It is cured and smoked, so it is not untreated raw fish, but it does not receive a full cooking heat treatment.

faq.question: Is hot-smoked salmon cooked?
faq.answer: Yes. Hot smoking uses enough heat to cook and coagulate the fish.

faq.question: Why is Listeria a concern?
faq.answer: Listeria can grow at refrigerator temperatures and can survive cold smoking because there is no final lethal cooking step.
